facts.question: How high is the 0 °C level in the next days, where does rain turn to snow, and is rain falling on the snowpack?
notes: 0 °C level = height where the air temperature crosses 0 °C (forecast, daily lowest and highest)
snow line = about 300 m below the 0 °C level, at the warmest hours of the day
rain-on-snow risk = snow on the slopes and a snow line above mid-mountain on a day with precipitation

en.title: High freezing level 5,313 ft (1,620 m) ends with Northeast snow
en.description: On November 10, the freezing level reaches 5,313 ft (1,620 m) above Northeast summits, bringing rain before 20–25 cm of snow arrives.
en.lede: Three of four Northeast ski resorts face a freezing level above their summits today, meaning rain is falling even at the peaks. By tomorrow, the freezing level drops sharply and 20–25 cm of snow arrives across Whiteface Mountain, Stratton, Okemo Mountain, and Magic Mountain.

p: The 0°C level—the height where air temperature crosses freezing—is currently between 2,750 and 5,970 ft (840–1,820 m) across the Northeast. At Whiteface Mountain, summit elevation 4,373 ft (1,333 m), it reached 5,313 ft (1,620 m) today: a 940 ft gap. When freezing stays that high, every drop of precipitation reaching the summit falls as rain, not snow, because the air is too warm for ice crystals to survive. The snow line—where wet snow transitions to rain—sits about 1,000 ft (300 m) below the 0°C level during the warmest hours. So at Whiteface, rain is falling right at the summit. At smaller Magic Mountain (top 2,850 ft / 869 m), the snow line climbed to 4,920 ft (1,500 m), meaning rain falls 2,070 ft above the peak. This is why freezing level is the first question in early season: it separates rain from snow, and determines whether incoming moisture builds base or melts existing cover.

sections.h: Today's pattern—no snow on the ground yet
p: This high freezing level brings an important caveat: there is currently no snow on the ground to have rain fall on. Regional coverage sits at just 110 km², with only one resort reporting measurable depth. The bare peaks mean today's rain is shedding off rock and soil into streams. The incoming 20–25 cm forecast for November 11–13 hasn't arrived yet, so the classic rain-on-snow hazard—where water percolates through new snow, adding weight and triggering instability—isn't present yet. This is timing luck: the warm, wet period (high freezing level, rain) is passing through before the new snow arrives. After November 11, as the freezing level drops and new snow lands on cold ground, conditions will reset. Early-season deposits build base; late-season deposits on thawing ground create surface problems. This one is falling at the right moment.

Here's where the forecast changes everything. November 11 brings a sharp cooling. The freezing level minimum drops to 2,460 ft (750 m), well below all four summits. At Stowe, the nearest weather station at 1,339 m elevation, model precipitation is 7 mm on November 11—and in this cold, dense air, all of it falls as snow. By November 12, the freezing level rebounds (maximum 6,035 ft / 1,840 m), but cold air is already in place, and the system is moving. The regional snapshot tells the story: today, 110 km² of snow, 1 resort with cover; November 13, 32,810 km², 62 resorts measurable. That's the speed of change when a cold front sweeps through. Early season in the Northeast is boilerplate: a sharp, brief transition from autumn warmth to winter cold.

The model forecast for November 11–13 is 20–25 cm at each resort: Whiteface 24 cm, Stratton 25 cm, Okemo and Magic 20 cm each. Currently all four have 0 cm on upper slopes. That fresh snow will land on mostly bare ground, except for a few thin patches left from the November 8–9 pulse (which added only 1–6 cm before melting). Early-season snow is characteristically dense and wet while air temperatures stay in the 1–5°C range; it will settle and compact within hours. At Magic Mountain (the lowest and smallest, 2,850 ft), 20 cm is meaningful base-building—the difference between skiable and closed. At Whiteface (highest, 4,373 ft), 24 cm might form a thinner cushion on steeper slopes. The timing coincides with cold air arrival, so snow quality will improve through the day as the system moves through and temperatures drop.

This model run is from November 10 and subject to change, as all forecasts are. The critical detail is the speed of the freezing level collapse on November 11—if the frontal passage is delayed, more moisture falls as rain at altitude; if it arrives on time, more transitions to snow. Regional precipitation data at three points shows: Tug Hill 15 mm total (mostly November 12), Stowe 16 mm (split between November 10–11), Buffalo 9 mm (November 12). Whiteface is likely to receive similar amounts. The forecast confidence for the basic pattern (cool-down, rain-to-snow transition, 20–25 cm accumulation) is moderate. If you're planning backcountry travel or off-piste skiing, check the official avalanche bulletin. Rain on new snow on steep slopes can be a hazard, even if quantities seem modest.

advice: Rain is falling on the summits today, above 4,265 ft (1,300 m) at Whiteface. Expect wet rock and slush. By November 11, the freeze level drops below the peaks and snow begins.
Incoming 20–25 cm will be heavy and wet at first, then improve in quality as air temperature drops through the day. Plan early morning skis, as mid-day visibility and corn may be issues.

Magic Mountain is the most exposed to marginal conditions today (rain down to 2,850 ft / 869 m), while Whiteface is least exposed (summit 4,373 ft / 1,333 m near the current freeze line). Choose your mountain accordingly.
The 24–25 cm forecast is an estimate for three days; don't expect all of it in one day. Watch local reports from each resort for real accumulation as the system moves through November 11–13.
Check the official avalanche bulletin if you are heading off-piste, especially after November 11 when new snow arrives on wet ground.

captions.map: Northeast freezing level on November 10 ranges from 2,750 ft (840 m) in the morning to 5,970 ft (1,820 m) by afternoon. By November 11, the minimum drops to 2,460 ft (750 m) as a cold front passes. Data from November 10 model run.
